name: Raleigh Speller
bio: Raleigh Speller was a Black man tried for rape in Williamston, North Carolina before all-white juries from which Negroes were barred, and repeatedly retried. He was executed in the gas chamber in 1953.
charges: Rape — a capital case tried before all-white juries from which Black jurors were barred.
convicted: Convicted of rape by all-white juries; executed 1953.

name: Charles Copeland
bio: Charles Copeland was a Black man convicted and sentenced to death in the electric chair on a rape charge in Jacksonville, Florida. His defenders called the case a racial frame-up.
charges: Rape — a capital conviction his defenders called a racial frame-up.
convicted: Convicted; sentenced to death.

name: Robert W. Burns
bio: Robert W. Burns was a Black serviceman convicted of rape-murder and sentenced to death by a U.S. military court on Guam in 1948, on a confession his defenders said was beaten out of him. New trials were denied.
charges: Rape-murder before a U.S. military court on Guam, on a confession his defenders said was coerced.
convicted: Convicted by a military court; death sentence.

name: Herman Dennis
bio: Herman Dennis was a Black Army private sentenced to death alongside Robert Burns by a U.S. military court on Guam in 1948 for rape-murder, on a coerced confession. His defenders called the case a frame-up.
charges: Rape-murder before a U.S. military court on Guam, on a coerced confession.
convicted: Convicted by a military court; death sentence.

name: Curtis Hopkins
bio: Curtis Hopkins was a Black man on trial for rape in Mississippi. His defenders called the case a racial frame-up.
charges: Rape — a capital charge his defenders called a racial frame-up.
convicted: Charged/tried for rape.

name: Jacob Jackson
bio: Jacob Jackson was a Black man in New York City convicted on a police counter-charge of assaulting an officer after he exposed police brutality. He faced up to a year in jail.
charges: Assaulting police — a counter-charge brought after he exposed police brutality.
convicted: Convicted on a police assault counter-charge.

name: Genevieve Jackson
bio: Genevieve Jackson was a Black woman in New York City convicted with Jacob Jackson on a police counter-charge of assaulting an officer after they exposed police brutality. She faced up to a year in jail.
charges: Assaulting police — a counter-charge brought after exposing police brutality.
convicted: Convicted on a police assault counter-charge.

name: Vernell Dieudonne
bio: Vernell Dieudonne was a Lincoln University student arrested in 1950 for refusing segregated theater seating. He and his fellow students won a civil-rights damages suit in 1953.
charges: Arrested in 1950 for refusing segregated theater seating.
convicted: Won a civil-rights damages suit in 1953.
sentence: Prevailed in a 1953 civil-rights damages suit.

name: Luther Manning
bio: Luther Manning was a Lincoln University student arrested in 1950 for refusing segregated theater seating. He and his fellow students won a civil-rights damages suit in 1953.
charges: Arrested in 1950 for refusing segregated theater seating.
convicted: Won a civil-rights damages suit in 1953.
sentence: Prevailed in a 1953 civil-rights damages suit.

name: Archibald Scales
bio: Archibald Scales was a Lincoln University student arrested in 1950 for refusing segregated theater seating. He and his fellow students won a civil-rights damages suit in 1953.
charges: Arrested in 1950 for refusing segregated theater seating.
convicted: Won a civil-rights damages suit in 1953.
sentence: Prevailed in a 1953 civil-rights damages suit.

name: Gabriel Parilla Fontanes
bio: Gabriel Parilla Fontanes was a Puerto Rican independence supporter and draft resister sought as a 'draft delinquent.' He fought a gun battle with FBI agents and police before being overcome with tear gas and arrested.
charges: Draft resistance — sought as a 'draft delinquent,' arrested after an armed standoff.
convicted: Arrested after an armed standoff with the FBI.
sentence: Prosecuted as a draft resister / independence militant.

name: Robert D. Walsh
bio: Robert D. Walsh was jailed in Michigan for refusing the induction oath, calling the Korean War 'not our war.' He was prosecuted as a conscientious objector.
charges: Refusing the induction oath, calling the Korean War 'not our war.'
convicted: Jailed for refusing the induction oath.

name: Joseph Ranchioni
bio: Joseph Ranchioni was a conscientious objector sentenced to three years for refusing to go to Korea on religious grounds. He was prosecuted in California.
charges: Refusing induction / refusing to go to Korea on religious grounds.
convicted: Convicted of refusing induction.

name: Caroline F. Urie
bio: Caroline F. Urie was an elderly Quaker who for years refused to pay the war portion of her federal income tax. She faced IRS enforcement over her war-tax resistance.
charges: War-tax resistance — refusing to pay the war portion of her federal income tax.
convicted: Civil war-tax resistance.

name: Earl King
bio: Earl King was a Marine Firemen's union official convicted of conspiracy in the 1936-37 Point Lobos case over a ship's engineer's death, in what supporters called a frame-up to break maritime unionism. He was sentenced to five-years-to-life and paroled after years in prison.
charges: Conspiracy in the Point Lobos engineer's death — a labor frame-up to break maritime unionism.
convicted: Convicted of conspiracy (a labor frame-up); 5-years-to-life.

name: Ernest Ramsay
bio: Ernest Ramsay was convicted of conspiracy in the 1936-37 Point Lobos frame-up, part of an effort his supporters said aimed to break maritime unionism. He was later offered freedom to falsely implicate Harry Bridges, which he refused.
charges: Conspiracy in the Point Lobos engineer's death — a labor frame-up.
convicted: Convicted of conspiracy (Point Lobos frame-up).

name: Frank Conner
bio: Frank Conner was a ship's oiler convicted of conspiracy in the 1936-37 Point Lobos frame-up, which supporters said was staged to break maritime unionism. He was sentenced to five-years-to-life and paroled.
charges: Conspiracy in the Point Lobos engineer's death — a labor frame-up.
convicted: Convicted of conspiracy (Point Lobos frame-up).

name: Dorothy Forest
bio: Dorothy Forest was a Communist Party defendant indicted in St. Louis in 1953 under the Smith Act. The Smith Act made it a crime to advocate overthrowing the government.
charges: Smith Act — indicted in St. Louis in 1953 as a Communist Party defendant.
convicted: Indicted under the Smith Act (1953).

name: James Forest
bio: James Forest was the Missouri Communist Party chairman, indicted in St. Louis in 1953 under the Smith Act. The Smith Act made it a crime to advocate overthrowing the government.
charges: Smith Act — indicted in St. Louis in 1953 as Missouri Communist Party chairman.
convicted: Indicted under the Smith Act (1953).

name: Marcus A. Murphy
bio: Marcus A. Murphy was a Black Communist Party defendant indicted in St. Louis in 1953 under the Smith Act. The Smith Act made it a crime to advocate overthrowing the government.
charges: Smith Act — indicted in St. Louis in 1953 as a Communist Party defendant.
convicted: Indicted under the Smith Act (1953).

name: James Edward Jackson
bio: James Edward Jackson was a prominent Black Communist leader indicted under the Smith Act who went underground as a 'refugee from political justice.' The Smith Act made it a crime to advocate overthrowing the government.
charges: Smith Act — indicted as a prominent Black Communist leader; went underground.
convicted: Indicted under the Smith Act; went underground.
sentence: Fugitive from a Smith Act indictment.

name: Vivian Hallinan
bio: Vivian Hallinan was tried with her husband, radical lawyer and Progressive Party candidate Vincent Hallinan, on income-tax-evasion charges widely seen as political. She was acquitted.
charges: Income-tax evasion — charges widely seen as political.
convicted: No — acquitted.

name: J. Minor Sullivan 3d
bio: J. Minor Sullivan 3d was a witness for the Trenton Six defense who was then hit with perjury warrants. Supporters called it retaliatory harassment.
charges: Perjury warrants brought after he testified for the Trenton Six defense.
convicted: Targeted with perjury warrants after testifying for the Trenton Six.

name: Carl Thierman
bio: Carl Thierman was a U.S. Army officer court-martialed at Fort Devens on a charge of obtaining his commission by concealing his political (Communist) associations. He was acquitted in 1953.
charges: Obtaining an Army commission by concealing his political (Communist) associations.
convicted: No — acquitted by court-martial (1953).
